query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The differences in mechanical properties between the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets can be attributed to variations in stacking fault energy (SFE) and the resulting effects on dislocation slip and mechanical twinning during deformation.
generation.intervention: Variation of constituent elements and their proportions
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with lower SFE will exhibit higher strength and ductility due to increased twinning-induced plasticity, while alloys with higher SFE will exhibit lower strength and ductility due to dominant dislocation slip
generation.boundary: Single-phase FCC structure, thermomechanical processing conditions
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between SFE, dislocation slip, and mechanical twinning in these alloys, as well as the effects of other microstructural features such as grain size and precipitates

falsification_experiment.design: In situ neutron diffraction and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) experiments to measure SFE and observe dislocation slip and mechanical twinning in the alloys during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the observed relationship between SFE, dislocation slip, and mechanical twinning does not match the predicted outcome, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The stacking fault energy (SFE), which is associated with chemical composition, is one of the most important parameters that influences activated deformation mechanisms, that is, dislocation slip, twinning, and martensitic transformation, during thermomechanical processing and recrystallization []. In low-SFE alloys, dislocations are dissociated into partials, and planar arrays of stacking faults would result in twinning or phase transformation. The improvement on the mechanical properties of Fe40.4Ni11.3Mn34.8Al7.5Cr6 alloy is attributed to the reduction of SFE from 22.2 mJ/m2 to 10.2 mJ/m2, and transition of the slip mode from wavy to planar slip, and micro-band induced plasticity activation []. Reza Razavi et al. suggested the addition of 1.3 wt.% Mo to Fe–33Mn–3Si–2Al twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steel to reduce the SFE, and increase the ultimate tensile strength and elongation []. Mo acts as a grain boundary stabilizer by forming (Fe, Mo)3C carbides and inhibiting grain coarsening.

AbstractIn this study, we manufactured a non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 high-entropy alloy (HEA) consisting of a single-phase face-centered-cubic structure. We applied in situ neutron diffraction coupled with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to investigate its tensile properties, microstructural evolution, lattice strains and texture development, and the stacking fault energy. The non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 HEA revealed a good combination of strength and ductility in mechanical properties compared to the equiatomic CoNiCrFe HEA, due to both stable solid solution and precipitation-strengthened effects. The non-equiatomic stoichiometry resulted in not only a lower electronegativity mismatch, indicating a more stable state of solid solution, but also a higher stacking fault energy (SFE, ~50 mJ/m2) due to the higher amount of Ni and the lower amount of Cr. This higher SFE led to a more active motion of dislocations relative to mechanical twinning, resulting in severe lattice distortion near the grain boundaries and dislocation entanglement near the twin boundaries. decision.trend: Research has been focused on understanding the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), particularly the effects of composition, processing, and microstructure on their behavior. Earlier studies have explored the properties of equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs, including their strength, ductility, and resistance to deformation and failure. Recent studies have also investigated the use of advanced characterization techniques, such as in situ neutron diffraction and electron backscattered diffraction, to study the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of HEAs.
decision.unsolved: The exact mechanisms underlying the differences in mechanical properties between equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs, as well as the effects of thermomechanical processing on their microstructure and properties, remain unclear. Additionally, the development of a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between composition, processing, and properties in HEAs is still an open question.
decision.lever: in situ neutron diffraction and electron backscattered diffraction
decision.why: To further understand the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of HEAs, particularly the effects of composition and thermomechanical processing on their behavior. This approach will allow for real-time monitoring of the microstructural changes and mechanical properties of HEAs during deformation and failure, providing valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms.
